title: Behind the Scenes at the Smithsonian: 150 Million Objects You've Never Seen
summary: Tucked away in Suitland, Maryland, is a treasure trove that few have seen: the Smithsonian's Museum Support Center (MSC). It holds nearly 150 million objects—meteorites older than Earth, alien-like worms in alcohol, a blue whale's jawbone, and even a freeze-dried crabeater seal that reportedly smells like burnt soy sauce. This is the backbone of the National Museum of Natural History, which displays only about 12,000 items at any time. The MSC consists of five storage pods, each the size of a football field and three stories high, with a sixth on the way. Inside, rows of cream-colored cabinets and miles of shelving preserve specimens under carefully controlled temperature and humidity. Security guards patrol 24/7, watching for power outages, floods, or even explosions from alcohol-filled jars. But this isn't just a giant closet. It's a vibrant research facility where scientists tackle big questions. For example, DNA from an African elephant stored here is helping researchers study a population that has long evaded humans. Decades ago, analysis of bird eggshells from the collection revealed that the pesticide DDT was thinning them, nearly driving bald eagles to extinction. That evidence helped lead to a U.S. ban on DDT in 1972. As museum director Kirk Johnson puts it, museums are 'vastly more vibrant and more important' than people think. The MSC is a 'forever' collection, safeguarding specimens for future scientists to study climate change, evolution, and biodiversity. So next time you visit a museum, remember: what you see is just the tip of the iceberg.
why_it_matters: These collections are like a library of life and Earth's history, holding irreplaceable evidence for solving modern problems like climate change and extinction. They remind us that science builds on past discoveries and that preserving nature — even in drawers — can protect our future.

background_read: The Smithsonian Institution (founded in 1846) is the world's largest museum, education, and research complex, headquartered in Washington, D.C. Its Museum Support Center in Suitland, Maryland, opened in 1983 to house overflow collections from the National Museum of Natural History and other museums. Only a tiny fraction of the 150 million objects are on public display; the rest form a permanent scientific archive. Collections like this have solved mysteries: the eggshell study that linked DDT (a widespread insecticide) to thin shells in bald eagles — the U.S. national bird — led to a nationwide ban in 1972 and the species' recovery. Other breakthroughs include using whale earwax plugs to study ocean pollution over time, or discovering new species hidden in jars for decades. Museum director Kirk Johnson emphasizes that these specimens are 'forever' resources, vital for tracking climate change, evolution, and the loss of biodiversity as the planet warms.

perspectives.description: The MSC safeguards a record of Earth's biodiversity, geology, and cultures for future generations. Its specimens have already led to major environmental wins like the DDT ban and continue to provide baseline data for climate research. This long-term thinking is essential for science.

Maintaining 150 million specimens is expensive, and many natural-history museums face budget cuts. Additionally, some older collections contain items acquired during colonial times under questionable circumstances, sparking debates about repatriation and ethical curation.

The vast gap between displayed objects (12,000) and stored ones (150 million) reveals how museums serve two distinct roles: public education and research. Most scientific work occurs behind the scenes, and the public's image of a museum as a static exhibit hall is incomplete. The DDT story illustrates how old samples can be reexamined with new technology and questions.

As DNA sequencing, isotope analysis, and imaging techniques advance, archived specimens become even more valuable. Researchers could reanalyze the MSC's meteorites for hints about the early solar system, or study the crabeater seal's tissues to understand past polar environments. The facility is building a sixth pod, anticipating future collections that will document our changing world.
